evidence: Cic. ND 2.27: aquae, quae effervēscunt subditīs ignibus (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Lewis & Short gives both senses, boil up and boil over. In Apicius honey boiling with wine threatens to boil over and settles when the fire is drawn off; he uses the parallel verb effervere. Cicero also has the word of a crowd boiling over with passion.

evidence: Vitr. 8.3.3: spīritibus extollēns operculum et crēscēns abundat
terms.comment: Vitruvius’s word for a covered pot whose water rises with the steam, lifts the lid, and runs over.

phrases.latin: nōn modo implet vās, sed spīritibus extollēns operculum et crēscēns abundat, sublātō autem operculō ēmissīs īnflātiōnibus in āere patentī rūrsus ad suum locum resīdit
phrases.english: it not only fills the pot but, lifting the lid with its steam, rises and boils over; take the lid off and let the steam out into the open air, and it settles back to its level

phrases.latin: sī effervere coeperit … subtractō ignī in sē redit
phrases.english: if it starts to boil over, … it settles down when the fire is drawn off

phrases.latin: Ecce, lac efferbuit! Cito, ignem subdūc.
phrases.english: Look, the milk has boiled over! Quick, take it off the heat.
Take the lid off, so the soup doesn’t boil over.

sources: Lewis & Short: effervesco · Lewis & Short: effervo · Lewis & Short: abundo
